source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact
finding: Founding method. Each pair of cited journals gets a z-score: how often the pair is co-cited versus a null built by randomly switching citation links while keeping citation counts. z<0 means atypical, z>0 conventional. Each paper is summarised by its median z (conventionality) and its 10th-percentile z (tail novelty).
numbers: 17.9 million Web of Science papers; 15,613 journals; over 122 million possible journal pairs. Fewer than 4% of papers have median z<0 (3.54% in 1980s, 2.67% in 1990s). About 40.8% (1980s) and 40.7% (1990s) have 10th-percentile z<0.
quote: Z scores below zero represent a journal pair that occurs less often than expected by chance
limits: Journal-level pairs only (domain level, not ideas). Impact is citations. Association, not cause. Reference lists are a proxy for what the author combined.
agent_relevance: Defines the one metric the whole subfield uses. Our agent needs a cheaper, text-based analogue, since journals do not exist for ideas.

source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact
finding: Main result. Papers with high median conventionality AND high tail novelty are hits about twice as often as the background rate. Papers high on only one of the two have about half that hit rate. Papers low on both are worst.
numbers: Hit = top 5% of citations at 8 years, WoS 1990-2000. Hit rate per 100 papers: conventional+tail-novel 9.11; conventional only 5.82; tail-novel only 5.33; neither 2.05; background 5. P<0.00001. Same pattern in 243 fields and for top 1% and top 10% hit definitions (supplement).
quote: novelty and conventionality are not opposing factors
limits: Impact measured by citations, which favour mainstream. Later work (Wang 2017, Lin 2022) shows the short window hides delayed payoffs of novel papers.
agent_relevance: Supports a mixed portfolio rule for open mode: mostly conventional attempts plus a small share of atypical ones, not all-atypical and not all-conventional.

source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact
finding: Teams insert atypical combinations into otherwise conventional knowledge more than solo authors do.
numbers: Teams 37.7% more likely than solo authors to have a novel combination in a conventional base (abstract). Team papers shifted the 10th-percentile z distribution toward novelty.
limits: Observational. Team size is confounded with field and topic.
agent_relevance: Suggests diversity of generators (different roles or different seeds) is where atypical parts come from, but see G4: samples from one model are not independent.

source: Lee, Walsh, Wang (2015) Creativity in scientific teams: unpacking novelty and impact
finding: Adapts the Uzzi score into a per-paper novelty measure (10th-percentile of pair commonness; novelty = minus log of commonness) and separates novelty from impact. Team size has an inverted-U relation with novelty but keeps rising with the chance of a high-impact paper. The size effect on novelty goes away once field variety or task variety is controlled.
numbers: Field variety vs novelty r=.25 (fine) and .26 (coarse); task variety vs novelty r=.18. Survey-linked sample of research projects; full-sample check on 9,428 cases.
limits: Survey respondents were about one-tenth SD less novel than non-respondents. Variety effects also show negative second-order terms: more variety helps only up to a point.
agent_relevance: Variety of knowledge sources helps novelty only up to a threshold. A cap on how many distant sources an attempt mixes is plausible.

source: Wang, Veugelers, Stephan (2017) Bias against novelty in science (NBER WP 22180 version)
finding: Different novelty measure: first-ever co-citation of two journals, weighted by how hard the combination is (cosine similarity of co-citation profiles). Highly novel papers are riskier and pay off later: more top-1% hits in the long run, more citations from other hits, cited by more fields, but fewer citations in a short window and lower-impact-factor journals.
numbers: 773,311 WoS articles from 2001, 14-year window. Highly novel vs non-novel: odds of top 1% (big hit) +39.82%; odds of being cited by big hits +26.20%; cited by 16.56% more subject categories; odds of top 10% +16.80% AND odds of bottom 10% +16.76% (higher variance). Highly novel papers are less likely to be top cited if window is under 3 years.
limits: One cohort (2001). Journal-level. Novelty score and Uzzi score are different constructs (see Bornmann 2019).
agent_relevance: Novel attempts have wide variance: higher mean tail but also more failures. Select on a held-out check, never on early signal. Early scores under-rate novel attempts.

source: Bornmann, Tekles, Zhang, Ye (2019) Do we measure novelty when we analyze unusual combinations of cited references?
finding: Convergent validity test of both reference-based scores against expert tags on F1000Prime. Uzzi/Lee score U mostly agrees with experts; Wang score W mostly does not.
numbers: Per one SD of U, expected count of the 'new finding' tag rises 7.47%. Logistic models for inclusion in F1000Prime (2013-2015, n=17,887; 14,345; 12,697): U coefficients 0.59 to 2.84, odds up more than 100% per SD; W mostly negative. Spearman between scores -0.05 to 0.1.
limits: Biomedicine only; F1000 papers skew to 'new finding' (70.21% carry that tag). A 2024 corrigendum exists (not read).
agent_relevance: Even the better metric (U) only partly matches expert judgement of novelty. Treat it as a weak proxy; novelty claims need a run-based check (G8).

source: Tahamtan and Bornmann (2018) Creativity in science and the link to cited references
finding: Interviews with corresponding authors of landmark scientometrics papers. Ideas often did not come from the cited literature. They came from practical problems, talks with colleagues and cross-field contact. Cited papers mainly placed the idea in context afterward.
numbers: Small case set of landmark papers in one field (scientometrics).
limits: Very small, one field. Self-report of origins is unreliable.
agent_relevance: Warns that the reference list is a record of positioning, not of where the idea came from; atypical citations may follow the idea rather than cause it.

source: Shibayama, Yin, Matsumoto (2021) Measuring novelty in science with word embedding
finding: Text-based Uzzi analogue: embed titles of cited references, compute pairwise distances, novelty = a high-quantile distance. Validated against co-citation distance, a questionnaire on self-reported newness, and top-1% citation.
numbers: Survey subset 321 biomedical respondents. Positive correlations with the self-reported newness score and non-significant or negative with the improvement score; title-based Novel1T00 still r=.170 (p<.01). Odds of top-1% rise with the quantile q; one distant pair can be enough. A second set of measures using only the focal document's own text failed (mostly insignificant or negative).
limits: Biomedicine. Correlations are modest. Needs the reference list, not the document alone.
agent_relevance: A cheap embedding-distance metric works as a proxy for combining distant parts. Usable inside the agent as a code-computed diversity signal, not a quality signal.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2022) New directions in science emerge from disconnection and discord
finding: Same Uzzi z-scores plus the D-index. Atypical papers are nearly twice as likely to disrupt, but disruption takes about ten years to stabilise. Atypicality also predicts later citation bursts (sleeping beauties). Mixed atypical-and-conventional best predicts being highly cited (confirms Uzzi), but disruption peaks at the highly atypical end.
numbers: Highly novel vs conventional papers: 61% vs 36% disruptive. Only 2.3% of papers are highly atypical; share fell from 3.9% (1970) to 1.4% (2000). Pearson r between typicality and D = -0.05 (p<0.001). Atypicality vs Sleeping Beauty Index r=0.08 (log-log). Cohorts 1970 (87,475 papers), 1980 (176,826), 1990 (318,914), 2000 (591,653); t-tests on disruptive-citation fraction 23.85 to 88.76. D-score reaches 80% of final value in about 10 years.
limits: Correlations are tiny even if significant. Stronger in computer science and engineering than natural sciences. This is the main CONFLICT with Li, Lin, Wu 2025, which finds a negative A-D link.
agent_relevance: Delay matters: a novel attempt cannot be judged by an early score. Wait for the held-out check, not first-look impressions.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2022) New directions in science emerge from disconnection and discord
finding: First computational model of atypicality: train word2vec skip-gram on co-cited journal sequences; the inner product of two journal vectors approximates the Uzzi z-score (a PMI view). Atypicality becomes distance in a learned knowledge space, which moves as yesterday's novelty becomes convention.
numbers: Correlation between z-score and journal-embedding inner product 0.74 (p<0.001). 50-dimension embeddings, negative sampling 5; 2,429 journals (1970 space), 8,009 (2000 space).
limits: Journal level only. Embedding is retrained per cohort.
agent_relevance: Gives a template: novelty = distance in an embedding of what has been co-used. Agent can compute distance between operator or idea components in code.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can recombination displace dominant scientific ideas? (arXiv 2506.15959 v4)
finding: Core paper of this subfield. Atypicality (Uzzi A-index) and disruption (D-index) capture different processes. Atypical work extends established concepts into new topics; disruptive work replaces a dominant idea within its own topic. H1: A and D are negatively correlated. H2: theories are harder to displace than methods.
numbers: 41 million articles 1965-2024 (abstract); about 40.9 million in the A-D analysis (1965-2020). Top 5% atypical papers A>22.9; top 5% displacing D>0.04. Negative A-D link in every discipline, period and team-size panel (95% bootstrap CIs). LLM test: Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct zero-shot labelled 50,147 highly cited D>0 papers as theory or method versus their top reference. Theory-type innovation probability falls as the gap between paper and reference grows. Example: Goedel 1931 to Turing 1937 quick; Milgram 1967 to Watts-Strogatz 1998 over three decades.
quote: Disruption, in contrast, signifies the replacement of a dominant idea within its own topic.
limits: Full text is short and gives no regression coefficients for A vs D (only binned plots). A-D link is correlational. LLM labelling robustness reported (few-shot, reworded options, a third 'others' option) without numbers.
agent_relevance: Direct basis for the operator rule: wide recombination and in-topic replacement are two different operators. Choose by goal: apply a known idea to a new area, or replace the incumbent answer to the same question.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can recombination displace dominant scientific ideas?
finding: Mechanism: functional equivalence. Displacement happens when a new idea does the same intellectual job as the incumbent, only better. Recombination joins complementary, distant things, so it rarely replaces anything. The paper's analogy: a 'microwave TV' may be creative but will not replace either appliance.
numbers: Examples: Turing machine replacing Goedel's symbolic model; Barabasi-Albert replacing Erdos-Renyi; Watson-Crick D=0.96 versus Human Genome draft D=-0.005.
limits: Argued by cases and a negative association, not an intervention test.
agent_relevance: Operator choice test for the schema: if the attempt must beat a specific incumbent answer, use a substitution operator that targets the same function. If exploring, use recombination.

source: Lin, Li, Wu (2025) The disruption index measures displacement between a paper and its most cited reference
finding: Math and data argument for what D measures. Rewrite D as a local displacement term dp=(Ni-Nj)/(Ni+Nj) and a knowledge burden term bp=Cmax/Cp (citations of the most cited reference over the paper's own). D is mostly determined by whether a paper beats its single most-cited reference. Reference citations follow a Zipf law, so the top reference dominates.
numbers: Zipf fit a=1.89, b=0.60 on 1,000 OpenAlex papers; mean Cmax/Ctotal 0.40 observed vs 0.42 predicted. 22 million papers with 10+ citations: 65% negative dp, 32% positive, 3% zero; 98.9% have bp>1; median bp=119; only about 1% have bp<1. 38% of 42 million papers have D>0; median D about -0.0001. Nobel prize papers (N=877) average D=0.1.
limits: Approximations (Ctotal about 2.5 Cmax). Authors are the creators of the D family, so this is not independent.
agent_relevance: D is a relative measure against a named incumbent. For our agent, 'disruptive' only has meaning relative to a chosen baseline answer.

source: Lin, Li, Wu (2025) The disruption index measures displacement between a paper and its most cited reference
finding: Validation by experts and by topic overlap. Expert nominations of disruptive papers have high D. High-D papers share a field with their most-cited reference far more than chance, so disruption is in-topic replacement.
numbers: Survey: 20 scholars, 190 responses; mean D of nominated disruptive papers 0.21 (top 1%), consolidating -0.011 (bottom 13%); AUC 0.83. For 49,077 papers with >100 citations and D>0.2, probability of sharing a field with the top reference 0.52 versus 0.014 expected by chance (37 times).
limits: Expert panel small and chosen by the authors; 292-category field taxonomy is coarse.
agent_relevance: Supports the split in the schema: in-topic displacement and cross-topic atypicality are separate and testable.

source: Lin, Li, Wu (2025) The disruption index measures displacement between a paper and its most cited reference
finding: Settles two disputes (from the D authors' side). Team size: Petersen et al. found a positive effect of team size on D with a 5-year window; with longer windows the negative effect of Wu et al. 2019 returns, turning at 10 years. Decline in D: Holst et al. said the decline is an artifact of zero-reference works; Lin et al. say their data had three times more zero-reference records.
numbers: Windows 1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 25 years with cohorts 47,129 to 536,463 papers; model on 1.7 million papers (1-10 authors, 5-50 refs, 10-1000 citations).
limits: Authors of D take sides. Park et al. 2025 rebut Holst et al. on the same points (see next).
agent_relevance: Window length changes the sign of conclusions: a short test window will mislead selection among attempts that pay off later.

source: Park, Leahey, Funk (2023) Papers and patents are becoming less disruptive over time (arXiv 2106.11184)
finding: CD index falls across all fields for papers and patents. Atypical-combination novelty also falls and narrower use of prior knowledge is linked to the decline.
numbers: 25 million WoS papers 1945-2010 and 3.5 million patents; replicated on JSTOR, APS, MAG, PubMed (20 million more papers). Average CD5 fell 91.9% (Social Sciences, 0.52 to 0.04) to 100% (Physical Sciences, 0.36 to 0) for papers; patents -78.7% to -91.5%. Watson-Crick CD5 0.62 vs Kohn-Sham -0.22. Title word diversity fell 76.5% to 88% in papers. Declining novelty in atypical combinations (Extended Data Fig 4).
limits: Contested: Holst et al. (2024) argue artifact of zero-reference works and citation inflation.
agent_relevance: Shows the atypicality-rise claim in Li 2025 is not a simple story: aggregate trends of both metrics are disputed, so do not tune an agent on those trends.

source: Park, Leahey, Funk (2025/2026) Robust evidence for declining disruptiveness: zero-backward-citation works
finding: Reply to Holst et al.'s critique. Using Holst's own data and exclusions, declines remain large and significant. Holst's data contain three times more zero-citation works, because about 20% of the sample is non-research content.
numbers: At least 2.8 million editorials, obituaries and comments, 1.5 million books and proceedings, 254,000 reviews. Non-research content fell from 40% to 8% of Holst's sample 1945-2010. Declining disruption is claimed in nearly 100 studies.
limits: Authors defend their own paper. No independent adjudicator read here.
agent_relevance: Illustrates that D-based claims depend on data cleaning. Use D only with checked data.

source: Larregue and Gingras (2026) The disruption index does not measure scientific innovation
finding: Validity critique of D. A positive D only means more later papers cite the focal paper alone than together with its references; it is a bibliographic shift, not proof of innovation. Country-level results look implausible.
numbers: A paper with only three citing papers can get D=1/3 (2 minus 1 over 3). Cui et al. 2026 data: 57.5% of Iraqi and 56% of Nigerian articles have D>0; India 34.3% (rank 26), China 26.9% (rank 66). Cites Wuestman et al. 2020: most breakthroughs follow an existing question and the state of the art.
limits: Opinion article on one paper (Cui et al. 2026); underlying Science paper not read.
agent_relevance: Caution: neither A nor D is a ground truth for 'good idea'. The agent should select by running, not by metric (G8).

source: Safari and Babaei (2026) Research novelty in Information Systems journals after ChatGPT
finding: Embedding-based relative novelty (distance from nearest recent predecessors in SPECTER2 space) fell more after 2022 for first authors in non-English-dominant countries than for English-dominant ones.
numbers: 13,847 articles, 44 A* and A IS journals, 2020-2025. Post x non-English-dominant interaction -0.176 SD (p<0.001), about 7 percentile points; with journal fixed effects -0.157. Same value across k=10, 15, 20 neighbours.
limits: LLM use not observed, so this is not an effect of LLMs. One field. Authors call one robustness check suggestive only.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence that LLM-assisted writing moves toward established frames, i.e. toward conventionality.

source: Hao, Xu, Li, Evans (2026) AI tools expand scientists' impact but contract science's focus (Nature; arXiv 2412.07727)
finding: Reported from a search summary only: scientists using AI tools publish more and get more citations, but the collective range of topics shrinks.
numbers: About 3 times as many papers and 4.8 times as many citations; topic range -4.63%; engagement between scientists -22%; 41 million OpenAlex papers; 311,000 AI-augmented (0.75%) (secondary summary).
limits: Not opened. Figures come from a news summary and a snippet; check the paper before use.
agent_relevance: If true, AI-aided work leans conventional or concentrates, which argues for forcing an explicit atypical share when the agent samples attempts.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Blind expert review: LLM-agent ideas are judged more novel than expert human ideas, and slightly less feasible. The agent's output lacks diversity, and LLM judges cannot rank ideas.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition; 79 reviewers. Novelty mean: human 4.84, AI 5.64, AI plus human rerank 5.81 (p<0.01, Welch tests with Bonferroni). Only about 5% of 4,000 seed ideas were non-duplicates (200) at cosine similarity 0.8. Reviewer agreement 56.1% (NeurIPS 2021 66.0%, ICLR 2024 71.9%). Best LLM judge (Claude-3.5 pairwise) 53.3%.
limits: NLP topics, prompting-based ideas, expert novelty ratings are noisy (56.1% agreement), and the follow-up paper shows the gap closes after execution.
agent_relevance: Directly supports G8: do not let a model rank novelty; and shows the generator collapses into duplicates, so diversity needs a code-side duplicate filter.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The ideation-execution gap
finding: Experts executed randomly assigned ideas (human or AI). After execution the AI ideas lose more score than human ideas on novelty, excitement, effectiveness and overall; some rankings flip.
numbers: 43 experts, over 100 hours each. Human ideas change in novelty -0.010, excitement +0.078, effectiveness -0.052; AI ideas drop 1.049, 1.760 and 1.879 on a 1-10 scale (p<0.05, FDR adjusted). After execution AI below human on excitement 3.90 vs 4.48 and effectiveness 4.13 vs 4.78 (not significant).
limits: Small sample (43 projects); NLP only; flips not significant.
agent_relevance: Idea-stage novelty judgments are inflated for LLM ideas. Run the idea, then judge (G8).

source: Liu, Dubova, Conklin, Harada, Griffiths (2026) Assessing the effect of cross-domain mapping on creativity in humans and LLMs
finding: Distant source-target pairs yield more original product ideas for both humans and LLMs. Humans benefit at nearly any distance; LLMs benefit only when the source is far enough and the model is strong. LLMs transfer structure and function, humans surface features.
numbers: 140 human designers and 7 LLMs; 1,002 raters for originality. Pooled over conditions, cross-domain mapping beta=0.36 (p<.001) with idea-source interaction 0.48; for o3 and Claude-Sonnet-4 no effect over all pairs (beta=0.02, p=.64), top 50% most distant 0.12 (p=.029), top 10% 0.24 (p=.024). LLM gap vs user-need vanishes once the closest 20% of pairs are dropped.
limits: Product design, not science; originality rated by lay raters; semantic distance from a Wikipedia-based embedding.
agent_relevance: Practical rule: when the agent forces a distant combination, make it really distant. Mild combinations gave no gain for LLMs and even hurt in the pooled result.

source: Shen, Druckmann, Zou (2026) Unlocking LLM creativity in science through analogical reasoning
finding: Cross-domain analogy retrieval (AR) counters mode collapse in LLM solution generation. Analogy-based solutions are far more diverse and more often novel than baselines.
numbers: Diversity metrics +90% to +173%; novel solutions over 50% of the time vs as low as 1.6% for baselines (Claude 1.6% < 21.6% < 50.4%; GPT 9.0% < 28.2% < 58.8%; Gemini 8.9% < 37.8% < 68.9%); 50 research problems. Human annotators called AR solutions more novel 78% of the time (kappa 0.445), but reasonable 67% vs 86% for the cross-domain baseline. LLM-human agreement up to 88.6% for domain distance, 75.7% for novelty.
limits: Novelty is judged mainly by an LLM and checked by modest human agreement. Reasonable rate falls (67%).
agent_relevance: A working recombination operator with a built-in distance measure. Pair it with an execution check because plausibility drops.

source: Gu, Wang, Zhang, Li (2024) LLMs can realize combinatorial creativity (arXiv 2412.14141)
finding: Framework implementing Boden's combinatorial creativity: generalisation-level retrieval for cross-domain knowledge, then a structured combine step. Similarity of generated ideas to real later research improved.
numbers: Gains of 7% to 10% in similarity scores across metrics on OAG-Bench.
limits: Abstract and introduction read; metric is similarity to real papers, which rewards predicting the mainstream, not novelty per se.
agent_relevance: Novelty without value is meaningless; the authors score against realised research, which is a form of held-out check.

source: Sinhahajari, Majumder, Poria (2026) On the limits of LLM-as-judge for scientific novelty assessment (RQ-Bench)
finding: LLM judges rate model-generated research questions as highly novel (a novelty mirage), while domain experts prefer the author-anchored real questions. Comparative judging makes LLM preference stronger.
numbers: gpt-5.5 non-obviousness win rate 27.2% standalone, 49.1% comparative. Humans favour author-anchored questions with win rates 78% and 56% for non-obviousness; LLM judges favour gpt-5.5 outputs at 82% and 52%. Agreement within humans 60%, within LLMs 52%, human-LLM as low as 22%. Many generated questions are narrow or source-bound.
limits: Small expert sample; research questions, not full ideas.
agent_relevance: Reconfirms G8 and G5: a model judge of novelty is not usable as selector.

source: Wu et al. (2026) NovBench: evaluating LLMs on academic paper novelty assessment
finding: Benchmark of LLM-written novelty evaluations against expert reviewer text, four dimensions (relevance, correctness, coverage, clarity). Current models show limited understanding of novelty; fine-tuned review models often fail instructions.
numbers: 1,684 paper-review pairs (abstract). Detailed scores not extracted.
limits: Only abstract and introduction read in detail; text-quality metric, not a novelty accuracy.
agent_relevance: Another sign that models cannot be trusted to say what is novel.

source: Foster, Rzhetsky, Evans (2015); Funk and Owen-Smith (2017); Wu, Wang, Evans (2019) Large teams develop and small teams disrupt
finding: Background works cited by the papers above, not opened here. Funk and Owen-Smith built the CD index; Wu et al. 2019 applied it and found small teams disrupt, large teams develop.
numbers: Wu 2019 numbers only via Lin 2025: negative team-size effect on D with long windows; Nobel papers average D 0.1.
limits: Not opened. Cited second-hand from opened papers.
agent_relevance: Used only for lineage.
